set1.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
set1.q: How does the nail bed feel when the fingers are clubbed?
opts: Tender and swollen
Clubbing is a bulbous swelling at the nail base, but its nail bed is described as spongy or floating, not tender.
Spongy or floating
Correct: in clubbing the nail bed feels spongy or floating, and the normal angle between the nail and proximal fold is lost.
Hard and fixed
That is the reverse of the clubbing finding; the clubbed nail bed feels spongy or floating.
Cold and pale
Coldness and pallor are color and temperature findings; clubbing is a spongy, floating nail bed with a lost nail angle.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set1.q: Which inspection findings fit asthma?
opts: Trachea midline, one side lagging
A midline trachea with unilateral decrease or delay in expansion fits pneumonia rather than asthma.
Tachypnea, dyspnea and retractions
Correct: asthma on inspection shows tachypnea or dyspnea and retractions, the visible work of breathing.
Narrowed intercostal spaces, trachea toward lesion
Narrowed intercostal spaces with ipsilateral tracheal deviation are the ATELECTASIS findings.
Asymmetric expansion, trachea pushed away
Asymmetric expansion with the trachea shifted to the unaffected side is a LARGE pleural effusion.

set1.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
set1.q: The finger on the right is shown beside a normal finger. Which condition is associated with the change it shows?
opts: Lung cancer
Correct: the right finger shows clubbing, a bulbous swelling of the soft tissue at the nail base, and clubbing is associated with lung cancer.
Asthma
Asthma is not associated with clubbing; the clubbing list includes lung cancer, interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is an acute air leak with no link to clubbing, which reflects longer-standing disease such as lung cancer.
Pleural effusion
A pleural effusion alters percussion and breath sounds, not the nails; clubbing is linked to lung cancer among others.
set1.alt: Two fingertips side by side in profile, each crossed by two measurement lines; the fingertip on the right has a bulbous, swollen nail base.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set1.q: How do rhonchi differ from wheezes?
opts: Grating; vanish when the breath is held
A grating sound that vanishes with a breath hold is a pleural rub, not rhonchi.
Lower in pitch; may clear with coughing
Correct: rhonchi are a variant of wheezes, lower in pitch, and may disappear with coughing, so secretions may be involved.
Higher in pitch; heard on inspiration
Rhonchi are LOWER in pitch than wheezes, and wheezes themselves can be inspiratory, expiratory or biphasic.
Discontinuous; from airways snapping open
Discontinuous sounds from small airways snapping open are crackles; rhonchi are continuous, like wheezes.

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: After multiple rib fractures, one area of the chest wall moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration. What is this?
opts: Unilateral respiratory lag
A lag is a delay in movement on one side (pleural disease, phrenic nerve injury), not inward motion on inspiration after fractures.
Traumatic flail chest

Correct: multiple rib fractures can cause paradoxical movement: as the diaphragm descends and intrathoracic pressure falls on inspiration, the injured area caves inward, and on expiration it moves outward.
Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is a spinal curvature with vertebral rotation that deforms the chest; it does not move paradoxically with breathing.
Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is a fixed depression of the lower sternum, present at rest, not a segment that moves the wrong way with each breath.
set1.alt: Outline of a chest cross-section with a solid line for expiration and a dashed line for inspiration; on inspiration one side of the chest wall bulges inward.

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set1.q: Sharp chest pain is worse lying supine and with inspiration, and improves when the patient sits forward. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
opts: Costochondritis
Costochondritis is localized and reproducible by palpation; position and leaning forward are not what define it.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Reflux pain is burning and postprandial; it worsens lying down but is not sharp and is not relieved by sitting forward.
Pericarditis
Correct: sharp, positional pain that is worse supine or with inspiration and improved by sitting forward points to pericarditis.
Pleuritis
Pleuritis gives sharp pain with inspiration or cough, but relief on sitting forward is the positional pattern of pericarditis.

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set1.q: Chest pain began abruptly, was at its worst from the start, and radiates to the back. Which diagnosis does this pattern suggest?
opts: Aortic dissection
Correct: sudden, tearing pain that is maximal early and radiates to the back is the pattern listed for aortic dissection.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is sudden too, but its pain is sharp and pleuritic, worse with inspiration or cough, rather than tearing to the back.
Myocardial infarction
Infarction gives retrosternal pressure or squeezing, often exertional, radiating to the arm, neck, jaw or back, not maximal at onset.
Pericarditis
Pericarditis is sharp and positional, worse supine and improved sitting forward, not abrupt tearing pain.

set1.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Where is the needle inserted for a thoracentesis?
opts: Anteriorly, in the 2nd intercostal space
The 2nd intercostal space anteriorly is for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax, not for draining fluid.
Laterally, between the 4th and 5th ribs
The space between the 4th and 5th ribs, in the triangle of safety, is the chest tube site rather than the thoracentesis site.
Posteriorly, just below the 8th rib
Entry just BELOW a rib meets the neurovascular structures that run along its inferior margin; the needle goes just above the 8th rib.
Posteriorly, just above the 8th rib
Correct: thoracentesis is done at T7-T8, the 7th intercostal space, with the needle immediately superior to the 8th rib, to drain a pleural effusion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set1.q: During a severe asthma attack, the wheezing becomes quieter while air movement is minimal. What does this indicate?
opts: Secretions cleared by coughing
Sounds that clear with coughing are rhonchi from secretions; fading wheeze with minimal air movement is the silent chest.
Air leaking into the pleural space
A pneumothorax gives absent sounds on one side with hyperresonance; diffusely fading wheeze in asthma is the silent chest.
A silent chest needing immediate action
Correct: wheezing becomes less audible as the airways narrow further; this silent chest of asthma means minimal air movement and needs immediate intervention.
The attack is beginning to resolve
Quieter wheezing here is not improvement: with minimal air movement it is the silent chest, which needs immediate intervention.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set1.q: Where may tactile fremitus be INCREASED in a large pleural effusion?
opts: Over the whole affected side
Over the effusion as a whole fremitus is decreased or absent; only toward its top may it rise.
Over the opposite lung
The effusion changes findings on its own side; the increase in fremitus is toward the top of the effusion.
Toward the top of the effusion
Correct: fremitus is decreased or absent over a large effusion but may be increased toward its top, where bronchial breath sounds may also be heard.
At the base of the effusion
Over the bulk of the fluid at the base fremitus is decreased or absent; the increase is toward the TOP.

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set1.q: Which item belongs to the detailed exposure history?
opts: Sputum color
Sputum color belongs to characterizing a productive cough (amount, color, consistency, odor, blood), not to the exposure history.
Morning headaches
Morning headache is one of the sleep questions asked about snoring and disordered sleep, not part of the exposure history.
Flights of stairs climbed
Flights of stairs measure the functional severity of dyspnea; the exposure history covers substances, occupation and travel.
Recent travel
Correct: the exposure history covers tobacco and nicotine, marijuana (smoked, vaped or ingested), recreational drugs, occupational and environmental exposures, and recent travel.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set1.q: An immunosuppressed patient has acute dyspnea with fever, chills, a productive cough and pleuritic pain. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Interstitial lung disease
Interstitial lung disease is gradually progressive with a dry cough, not acute with fever and sputum.
Pneumonia
Correct: pneumonia is acute onset with fever, chills, cough, sputum and pleuritic pain, after recent illness, aspiration risk or immunosuppression.
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is sudden unexplained dyspnea with hemoptysis, syncope or leg symptoms; fever, chills and sputum point to pneumonia.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax gives sudden unilateral pleuritic pain without fever, chills or sputum.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set1.q: Which history raises suspicion for pulmonary embolism in a patient with sudden dyspnea?
opts: Cold air and exercise as triggers
Cold air, exercise and allergens are asthma triggers; asthma is episodic rather than sudden and unexplained.
Estrogen use and recent immobility
Correct: the relevant history for pulmonary embolism is prior venous thromboembolism, surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen and pregnancy or the postpartum period.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is relevant history for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which is slowly progressive.
Autoimmune disease on new medication
Autoimmune disease and medications are the history for interstitial lung disease, which is gradually progressive.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set1.q: In which position is the mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign) best heard?
opts: Sitting, leaning forward
Sitting forward is what relieves pericarditis pain; the mediastinal crunch is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position.
Sitting, arms folded
Sitting with arms folded is the position for the posterior lung examination, not for hearing the crunch.
Supine
Supine is used for the anterior chest examination; the crunch is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position.
Left lateral decubitus
Correct: the mediastinal crunch, precordial crackles in time with the heartbeat, is best heard with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set1.q: A grating, creaking sound over the lower lateral chest is heard in both phases of breathing and disappears when the patient holds their breath. Which sound is it?
opts: Mediastinal crunch
The mediastinal crunch is crackles synchronized with the heartbeat, not with respiration, so it would persist during a breath hold.
Coarse crackles
Coarse crackles are popping sounds from secretions or fluid that do not depend on the pleura and are not described as grating.
Pleural rub
Correct: a pleural rub is discontinuous, low-frequency and grating, usually biphasic, and disappears with a breath hold, which separates it from a pericardial friction rub.
Pericardial friction rub
A pericardial friction rub follows the heart, so it does NOT disappear when the breath is held; that is the distinguishing test.

mis.Pericardial friction rub: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Mediastinal crunch: ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Pain on deep inspiration comes from irritation of which layer?
opts: Parietal pleura
Correct: the parietal pleura is highly innervated by intercostal and phrenic nerves, so irritating it produces pleuritic pain with deep inspiration.
Visceral pleura
The visceral pleura covers the lung surface and lacks sensory nerves, so irritation of it is not the source of pleuritic pain.
Alveolar walls
The alveoli are the site of gas exchange; pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura with its intercostal and phrenic nerve supply.
Bronchial lining
The bronchi carry air to the alveoli; pain with deep inspiration comes from irritation of the parietal pleura.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set1.q: A patient with sudden dyspnea has a history of emphysema and a recent procedure, and reports abrupt pain on one side of the chest. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is also sudden, but its history is prior clots, surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen or pregnancy rather than emphysema.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is acute with fever, chills, cough and sputum after illness or aspiration, not abrupt one-sided pain after a procedure.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic wheezing with allergen and exercise triggers, not abrupt unilateral pain after a procedure.
Pneumothorax
Correct: pneumothorax is sudden dyspnea with abrupt unilateral pleuritic pain, after trauma, a recent procedure, emphysema or a prior pneumothorax.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set1.q: Over the right lower chest there is dullness, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds and egophony, and the trachea is midline. Which condition fits?
opts: Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is hyperresonant or tympanic with decreased or absent fremitus, not dull with increased fremitus.
Pneumonia
Correct: pneumonia gives dullness over the airless area, increased fremitus, bronchial sounds, late inspiratory crackles and positive transmitted voice sounds, with a midline trachea.
Pleural effusion
An effusion is dull too, but it DECREASES fremitus and breath sounds over the fluid.
Atelectasis
Atelectasis is dull with DIMINISHED fremitus and pulls the trachea toward the affected side.

mis.Pleural effusion: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Atelectasis: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Pneumothorax: ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: When egophony is present, how does the patient's spoken "ee" sound through the stethoscope?
opts: Like a louder "ninety-nine"
A louder "ninety-nine" is a positive BRONCHOPHONY result; egophony uses "ee".
Like a clear whisper
Louder, clearer whispered sounds are positive whispered pectoriloquy, a different test.
Like "a"
Correct: with egophony the spoken "ee" sounds like "a" (or "ay"); over normal lung it is heard as a muffled long E.
Like a muffled long "ee"
A muffled long E is what you hear when egophony is NOT present, over normal air-filled lung.

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: A silent gap between inspiration and expiration suggests which breath sound?
opts: Bronchial
Correct: a silent gap between inspiration and expiration suggests bronchial breath sounds, which out at the bases mean consolidated or fluid-filled lung.
Vesicular
Vesicular sounds are the normal sounds over most of the lung, soft and low-pitched, not marked by a silent gap.
Bronchovesicular
Bronchovesicular sounds have inspiration and expiration about equal with intermediate pitch; the gap points to bronchial sounds.
Tracheal
Tracheal sounds are heard over the neck and are very loud; the silent gap is the clue named for bronchial sounds.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set1.q: Diminished chest wall motion, narrowed intercostal spaces and a trachea deviated toward the same side suggest which condition?
opts: Large pleural effusion
A large effusion shifts the trachea to the UNAFFECTED side and causes asymmetric expansion.
Tension pneumothorax
A tension pneumothorax shifts the trachea toward the UNAFFECTED side, the opposite of this patient.
Lobar pneumonia
In pneumonia the trachea stays midline, with increased fremitus and bronchial sounds over the involved area.
Atelectasis
Correct: atelectasis shows diminished chest wall motion, narrowed intercostal spaces and ipsilateral tracheal deviation, with dullness over the affected side.

mis.Lobar pneumonia: ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set1.q: Which percussion note over the affected side fits a pneumothorax?
opts: Hyperresonant or tympanic
Correct: a pneumothorax is hyperresonant or tympanic over the affected side, with decreased or absent fremitus and breath sounds.
Dull
Dullness means fluid or solid tissue, as in pleural effusion, pneumonia or atelectasis, not air in the pleural space.
Resonant and symmetric
Resonant, symmetric notes are the NORMAL finding; a pneumothorax is hyperresonant on one side.
Dull with a high diaphragm
Dullness with high diaphragmatic excursion is the pleural effusion pattern.

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Over normal air-filled lung, how do the patient's whispered words come through?
opts: Changed from "ee" to "ay"
"Ee" heard as "ay" is egophony, a sign of consolidation, and uses the spoken voice rather than a whisper.
Muffled but louder than speech
Over normal lung both spoken and whispered words are muffled and indistinct; a whisper is fainter, not louder.
Faint and indistinct, if heard at all
Correct: over normal lung whispered words are faint and indistinct, if heard at all; over consolidated lung they are louder and clearer.
Louder and clearer than expected
Louder, clearer whispered sounds are POSITIVE whispered pectoriloquy, a sign of consolidation.

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Which chest wall deformity may compress the heart and great vessels and cause murmurs?
opts: Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Correct: in funnel chest the lower sternum is depressed, and compression of the heart and great vessels may cause murmurs.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest pushes the sternum forward, away from the heart, so it is not the deformity linked to murmurs.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest is an increased anteroposterior diameter, normal in infancy and common with aging and obstructive lung disease.
Traumatic flail chest
Flail chest is paradoxical movement of a fractured rib segment, not compression of the heart.

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set1.q: A patient coughs up large amounts of foul-smelling sputum every day. Which conditions does this suggest?
opts: Cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis
Correct: COPIOUS foul-smelling sputum is the pattern for cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis; foul smell alone suggests an anaerobic lung abscess.
Viral infection or postnasal drip
Viral infection and postnasal drip give mucoid sputum: translucent, white or gray, and not foul-smelling.
Bacterial pneumonia or bronchitis
Bacterial pneumonia is the purulent pattern, yellow or green; copious and foul-smelling points elsewhere.
Asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Asthma brings wheezing, cough and chest tightness, and the obstructive disease scant sputum, not a daily copious foul load.

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set1.q: Which duration defines a chronic cough?
opts: More than 2 weeks
Two weeks is still acute; acute cough runs up to 3 weeks and chronic begins beyond 8 weeks.
More than 3 weeks
Beyond 3 weeks a cough is SUBACUTE; chronic begins only after 8 weeks.
More than 8 weeks
Correct: cough is acute under 3 weeks, subacute at 3-8 weeks and chronic beyond 8 weeks.
More than 12 weeks
The threshold is lower: a cough lasting more than 8 weeks is already chronic.

set1.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
set1.q: Which feature suggests that blood brought up by a patient came from the stomach rather than the respiratory tract?
opts: Blood streaks after throat clearing
Blood streaks can come from the nose, mouth or pharynx; darker blood with food particles is what points to the stomach.
Bright red blood after a coughing fit
Blood coughed up from the chest points to the lower respiratory tract; stomach blood is darker and mixed with food.
Blood following a nosebleed
Nasopharyngeal blood can be aspirated and then coughed out; it is not darker or mixed with food the way gastric blood is.
Darker blood mixed with food particles
Correct: blood from the stomach is darker than respiratory blood and comes with food particles, and vomited blood is likely gastrointestinal.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set1.q: Dyspnea comes in episodes with symptom-free intervals, is often worse at night, and is triggered by cold air and exercise. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is sudden, unexplained dyspnea, not a recurring episodic pattern triggered by cold air and exercise.
Asthma
Correct: asthma is episodic with symptom-free intervals, often worse at night, with wheezing, cough and chest tightness and triggers such as allergens, exercise and cold air.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
This disease is slowly progressive exertional dyspnea without symptom-free intervals; episodic dyspnea with clear gaps is asthma.
Interstitial lung disease
Interstitial lung disease is gradually progressive exertional dyspnea with a dry cough, not episodes separated by normal intervals.

set1.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Why are needles and tubes placed just over the superior margin of a rib?
opts: Neurovascular structures run along each rib's upper edge
That reverses it: the neurovascular structures run along the INFERIOR margin, which is why entry is at the superior margin of the rib below.
The parietal pleura is absent just below each rib
The parietal pleura lines the whole inner rib cage and the upper diaphragm; the rule exists to avoid the neurovascular structures under each rib.
The costal cartilage blocks access below each rib
Costal cartilage joins ribs to the sternum anteriorly; the reason for the superior-margin rule is the neurovascular bundle on each rib's lower edge.
Neurovascular structures run along each rib's lower edge
Correct: the neurovascular structures run along the inferior margin of each rib, so going in just above the rib below avoids them.

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set1.q: Bronchial breath sounds are heard over the lung bases, where vesicular sounds are expected. What does this suggest?
opts: Hyperinflated lung
Hyperinflated lung, as in obstructive disease, gives decreased or distant breath sounds, not bronchial sounds.
A pneumothorax
A pneumothorax gives decreased or absent breath sounds with hyperresonance, not bronchial sounds at the bases.
Consolidated or fluid-filled lung
Correct: bronchovesicular or bronchial sounds in unexpected places mean air-filled lung has been replaced by fluid-filled or consolidated tissue, as in lobar pneumonia.
A normal variant at the bases
Bronchial sounds are normal only over the manubrium; at the bases they are abnormal and suggest consolidation.

set2.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Aspirated material most often enters the right bronchial tree. Which feature of the right main bronchus explains this?
opts: It is narrower
The right main bronchus is WIDER, not narrower, and more vertical, which is why aspirated material favors it.
It passes under the aortic arch
The LEFT main bronchus passes beneath the aortic arch before entering the left hilum; the right is the more vertical one.
It is more vertical
Correct: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so aspirated material more commonly enters the right bronchial tree.
It is longer
Length belongs to the LEFT main bronchus, which is longer and more horizontal; the right is shorter and more vertical.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set2.q: How do coarse crackles differ from fine crackles?
opts: They disappear when the breath is held
Disappearing with a breath hold separates a pleural RUB from a pericardial friction rub; it does not separate crackles.
They are higher pitched and softer
That reverses them: coarse crackles are LOUDER and LOWER in pitch; fine crackles are the soft, high-pitched ones.
They are continuous and musical
Both kinds of crackle are non-musical and discontinuous; continuous musical sounds are wheezes.
They do not change with body position
Correct: coarse crackles are louder, lower in pitch, start early in inspiration and last through expiration, and do not change with position (larger airway secretions or fluid).

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set2.q: Which palpation finding fits lobar pneumonia?
opts: Absent tactile fremitus
Decreased or absent fremitus fits pneumothorax and pleural effusion, where air or fluid separates lung from chest wall.
Trachea pushed to the other side
A trachea shifted toward the unaffected side fits a tension pneumothorax or a large effusion; in pneumonia it is midline.
Trachea pulled toward the lesion
Ipsilateral tracheal deviation is the atelectasis finding; in pneumonia the trachea stays midline.
Increased tactile fremitus
Correct: pneumonia increases tactile fremitus over the consolidation, with a unilateral decrease or delay in chest expansion.

set2.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
set2.q: Which non-pulmonary condition is associated with clubbing?
opts: Inflammatory bowel disease
Correct: beyond the lung diseases, clubbing is seen in inflammatory bowel disease, congenital heart disease and malignancy.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Reflux is a cause of burning chest pain and of cough, not of clubbing; inflammatory bowel disease is the bowel condition linked to it.
Hypertension
Hypertension is relevant history for left-sided heart failure, not a cause of clubbing.
Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is a transudative cause of pleural effusion, not a disease associated with clubbing.

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Cyanosis of the lips, tongue and oral mucosa signals what?
opts: Hypoxia
Correct: cyanosis in the lips, tongue and oral mucosa signals hypoxia, and is looked for with skin and nail color during the survey.
Acute coronary syndrome
Pallor and diaphoresis are the color changes common in acute coronary syndrome and heart failure; central cyanosis signals hypoxia.
Upper airway obstruction
Upper airway obstruction is signaled by stridor, a high-pitched inspiratory whistle over the neck, not by cyanosis as such.
Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is associated with clubbing of the nails, not defined by cyanosis of the lips and tongue, which signals hypoxia.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set2.q: Episodes of air hunger, sighing, lightheadedness and tingling around the mouth occur at rest during emotional distress. What should be done before attributing them to anxiety?
opts: Confirm symptoms occur at rest
Hyperventilation can occur at rest or with distress either way; medical causes still have to be considered first.
Confirm a history of distress
Emotional distress may contribute, but it does not make anxiety the cause until medical causes have been considered.
Consider medical causes first
Correct: this is hyperventilation, and although anxiety may contribute, medical causes must be considered first.
Confirm tingling is present
Perioral and extremity tingling is part of hyperventilation itself and does not exclude a medical cause.

mis.Confirm tingling is present: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Confirm symptoms occur at rest: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: What is the main limitation of chest percussion?
opts: It cannot detect a pleural effusion
A pleural effusion is detected as dullness over the fluid, with a high level of diaphragmatic excursion.
It cannot detect deep-seated lesions
Correct: percussion shows whether underlying tissue is air-filled, fluid-filled or consolidated, but it cannot help with deep-seated lesions.
It cannot tell air from fluid
Telling air-filled from fluid-filled or consolidated tissue is exactly what percussion does; its limit is deep-seated lesions.
It cannot detect a pneumothorax
A large pneumothorax is detected as unilateral hyperresonance or a tympanic note on the affected side.

set2.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Which structure forms the posterior border of the triangle of safety?
opts: The scapular line
The scapular line is a posterior vertical reference line on the back, not a border of the triangle, which lies in the midaxillary line.
Lateral border of the latissimus dorsi
Correct: the triangle is bounded by the latissimus dorsi posteriorly, the pectoralis major anteriorly and the nipple line (4th or 5th intercostal space) below.
Lateral border of the pectoralis major
The pectoralis major forms the ANTERIOR border of the triangle; the posterior border is the lateral edge of the latissimus dorsi.
The nipple line
The nipple line, at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, is the INFERIOR boundary; the posterior border is the latissimus dorsi.

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: A hospitalized patient is too weak to sit up for the posterior chest examination. How should the back be examined?
opts: Examine the anterior chest and skip the back
The posterior chest is not skipped; rolling the patient to each side lets you percuss and auscultate the back in turn.
Auscultate the back through the gown
Clothes and paper gowns produce sounds, so the patient is de-robed; rolling to each side gives access to the back.
Wait until the patient can sit upright
There is no need to defer: rolling the patient to one side, then the other, completes the posterior examination.
Roll the patient to one side, then the other
Correct: the posterior chest is ideally examined sitting, arms folded; if that cannot be done, roll the patient to one side and then the other, percussing and auscultating in each position.

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set2.q: Translucent, white or gray sputum is seen more in which setting?
opts: Bacterial pneumonia
Bacterial pneumonia gives purulent sputum, yellow or green, rather than translucent white or gray mucoid sputum.
Anaerobic lung abscess
An anaerobic lung abscess gives foul-smelling sputum; translucent white or gray sputum is mucoid.
Cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis
Cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis produce copious foul-smelling sputum, not translucent white or gray mucoid sputum.
Viral infection or postnasal drip
Correct: translucent, white or gray sputum is mucoid sputum, seen more in viral infections and postnasal drip.

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set2.q: A patient's sputum has a foul smell. Which condition does foul-smelling sputum suggest?
opts: Postnasal drip
Postnasal drip produces mucoid, translucent sputum, not foul-smelling sputum.
Anaerobic lung abscess
Correct: foul-smelling sputum suggests an anaerobic lung abscess; when it is also copious, think cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis.
Viral bronchitis
Viral infections give mucoid sputum, translucent white or gray, without the foul smell.
Bacterial pneumonia
Bacterial pneumonia is signaled by purulent yellow or green sputum, not by a foul odor.

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set2.q: Which question assesses the functional severity of dyspnea?
opts: What makes it better or worse?
Triggers and relievers characterize dyspnea; functional severity asks about stairs, distance and daily tasks.
How many flights of stairs can you climb?
Correct: functional severity is graded by walking distance, flights of stairs without stopping, everyday tasks and change from baseline.
Did it start suddenly or gradually?
Sudden or gradual is the ONSET of the symptom, which characterizes dyspnea rather than measuring its functional severity.
Is it worse when you lie flat?
Body position is part of characterizing the symptom; severity is measured by what the patient can still do.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set2.q: A patient with an autoimmune condition has gradually progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, fatigue and weakness. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Asthma
Asthma is episodic with symptom-free intervals and wheezing, not steadily progressive with a dry cough.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is sudden, with abrupt unilateral pleuritic pain, not gradually progressive.
Interstitial lung disease
Correct: gradually progressive exertional dyspnea with dry cough, fatigue and weakness, in autoimmune disease or after medication or occupational exposure, is interstitial lung disease.
Chronic bronchitis
Chronic bronchitis starts with a chronic PRODUCTIVE cough and sputum; this cough is dry.

mis.Chronic bronchitis: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Which chest shape is shown?
opts: Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is a depression of the lower sternum, not an evenly rounded chest with a wide anteroposterior diameter.
Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is an abnormal spinal curvature with vertebral rotation that deforms the chest asymmetrically.
Barrel chest
Correct: the cross-section is nearly round, with an increased anteroposterior diameter; normal in infancy, and it often accompanies aging and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest has the sternum displaced forward with the adjacent costal cartilages depressed, a pointed rather than rounded profile.
set2.alt: Outline of a chest cross-section that is almost round, beside a side view of a man whose chest is deep from front to back.

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Which muscles contract during INSPIRATION when accessory muscles are being used?
opts: Intercostals and abdominal obliques
Those contract during EXPIRATION; the inspiratory accessory muscles are the sternocleidomastoid and scalene.
Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
Those two muscles border the triangle of safety for chest tubes; the inspiratory accessory muscles are the sternocleidomastoid and scalene.
Scalenes and abdominal obliques
The abdominal obliques work in expiration; inspiration recruits the sternocleidomastoid together with the scalenes.
Sternocleidomastoid and scalenes
Correct: the sternocleidomastoid and scalene contract during inspiration; the intercostals and abdominal obliques contract during expiration.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set2.q: A patient with hypertension and a prior myocardial infarction has dyspnea that is worse lying flat, with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema and weight gain. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pneumonia
Pneumonia is acute with fever, chills, sputum and pleuritic pain, not edema and weight gain after a myocardial infarction.
Left-sided heart failure
Correct: left-sided heart failure can be gradual or sudden, worse with exertion or lying flat, with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, edema and weight gain.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic wheezing, worse at night but with symptom-free intervals, and does not bring edema and weight gain.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
This disease is slowly progressive exertional dyspnea after smoking or exposures; orthopnea, edema and weight gain point to the heart.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set2.q: A series of precordial crackles keeps time with the heartbeat rather than with breathing, in a patient with severe central chest pain. What does this suggest?
opts: Air in the mediastinum
Correct: this is the mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign), from air entering the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum).
Inflamed pleura
Inflamed pleura give a pleural rub, which follows respiration and disappears with a breath hold, not the heartbeat.
Interstitial fibrosis
Fibrosis gives fine inspiratory crackles over the lung that follow breathing and change with body position.
Air in the pleural space
A pneumothorax gives decreased or absent breath sounds and hyperresonance, not crackles in time with the heart.

set2.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
set2.q: Which nail finding defines clubbing?
opts: Loss of the nail-to-fold angle
Correct: clubbing is a bulbous swelling at the nail base with loss of the normal angle between the nail and the proximal nail fold.
Blue color of the nail beds
Blue color is cyanosis, judged at the lips, tongue and oral mucosa as a sign of hypoxia; clubbing is a change in shape.
Pallor of the nail beds
Pallor, with diaphoresis, is common in heart failure and acute coronary syndrome; clubbing is loss of the nail angle.
A hard, fixed nail bed
The clubbed nail bed is the opposite: it feels spongy or floating, with loss of the nail-to-fold angle.

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Which chest wall deformity do these two views show?
opts: Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Correct: the sternum is displaced anteriorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter, and the costal cartilages next to it are depressed.
Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is the reverse: a depression in the lower sternum rather than a sternum pushed forward.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest raises the anteroposterior diameter evenly with a rounded outline, without a forward-pointing sternum.
Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is a curvature and rotation of the spine that deforms the chest; the sternum is not pushed forward.
set2.alt: Outline of a chest cross-section that comes to a point at the front, with the sternum pushed forward and the cartilages beside it pressed in, beside a side view of a boy's chest.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set2.q: A high-pitched inspiratory whistling is heard over the neck without a stethoscope. What does it signal?
opts: Secretions in large airways
Secretions give rhonchi, which may clear with coughing; whistling over the neck on inspiration is stridor.
Upper airway obstruction
Correct: high-pitched inspiratory whistling is stridor, from obstruction in the larynx or trachea, and it needs urgent evaluation and immediate intervention.
Lower airway narrowing
Lower airway narrowing produces wheezes, expiratory or continuous, over the lung; stridor is upper airway obstruction.
Inflamed pleural surfaces
Inflamed pleura give a grating pleural rub over the axilla and bases, not inspiratory whistling over the neck.

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Dullness to percussion over the lung means what?
opts: Air has entered the pleural space
Air in the pleural space (a large pneumothorax) gives UNILATERAL hyperresonance, the opposite of dullness.
A large air-filled bulla is present
An air-filled bulla gives unilateral hyperresonance; dullness means air has been replaced by fluid or solid tissue.
Fluid or solid tissue has replaced air
Correct: dullness means fluid or solid tissue has replaced the air, as in lobar pneumonia, pleural effusion, hemothorax, empyema, fibrous tissue or tumor.
The lung is hyperinflated
Hyperinflated lung, as in asthma or obstructive lung disease, gives generalized HYPERRESONANCE, not dullness.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set2.q: In which type of atelectasis may fremitus be increased and adjacent tracheal sounds be transmitted?
opts: Left upper lobe atelectasis
The exception named is on the RIGHT, in the upper lobe next to the trachea; the left upper lobe is not singled out.
Right upper lobe atelectasis
Correct: atelectasis usually diminishes fremitus and abolishes breath sounds, except in right upper lobe atelectasis, where fremitus may be increased and adjacent tracheal sounds transmitted.
Right lower lobe atelectasis
The exception is the right UPPER lobe, beside the trachea; lower lobe atelectasis follows the usual pattern of diminished fremitus.
Left lower lobe atelectasis
Left lower lobe atelectasis follows the usual rule: diminished fremitus and absent sounds while the plug persists.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set2.q: Over the left lower chest there is dullness, decreased fremitus and absent breath sounds, with bronchial sounds near the top of the dull area, and the trachea is shifted to the right. Which condition fits?
opts: Large left pleural effusion
Correct: a large effusion is dull over the fluid with decreased or absent fremitus and breath sounds, bronchial sounds near its top, and the trachea shifted to the unaffected side.
Left lower lobe pneumonia
Pneumonia is dull too, but it INCREASES fremitus over the area and leaves the trachea midline.
Left lower lobe atelectasis
Atelectasis pulls the trachea toward the LEFT, the affected side, not to the right.
Left tension pneumothorax
A tension pneumothorax shifts the trachea away too, but it is hyperresonant, not dull.

mis.Left lower lobe pneumonia: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Left lower lobe atelectasis: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Left tension pneumothorax: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set2.q: After a recent procedure, a patient with emphysema has decreased tactile fremitus, hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on one side, and the trachea is midline. Which condition fits?
opts: Pneumothorax
Correct: decreased or absent fremitus, a hyperresonant or tympanic note and decreased or absent breath sounds on one side are the pneumothorax findings; the trachea shifts only with tension.
Pleural effusion
An effusion also lowers fremitus and breath sounds, but it is DULL to percussion, not hyperresonant.
Atelectasis
Atelectasis is dull with ipsilateral tracheal deviation, not hyperresonant.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is dull with INCREASED fremitus and bronchial breath sounds.

mis.Pleural effusion: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Atelectasis: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Pneumonia: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
set2.q: What produces crackles?
opts: Airflow through a narrowed upper airway
Airflow through a narrowing in the upper respiratory tract produces STRIDOR, best heard over the neck on inspiration.
Roughened pleural layers sliding together
Inflamed visceral and parietal pleura sliding against each other produce a pleural RUB, grating and biphasic.
Small airways snapping open on inspiration
Correct: crackles are non-musical, discontinuous sounds made when deflated small airways abruptly snap open during inspiration.
Rapid airflow through nearly closed bronchi
Rapid airflow through bronchi narrowed almost to closure produces WHEEZES, which are continuous and musical.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
set2.q: Which auscultatory findings fit asthma?
opts: Absent sounds over a bronchial plug
Absent sounds while a bronchial plug persists are the atelectasis finding.
Wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase
Correct: asthma gives wheezes, possibly crackles, and a prolonged expiratory phase.
Bronchial sounds with egophony
Bronchial sounds with egophony over an involved area are the pneumonia (consolidation) findings.
Absent breath sounds with a pleural rub
Decreased or absent sounds with a possible pleural rub are the pneumothorax or effusion findings.

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set2.q: A patient reports musical breathing sounds that others can hear. What produces this symptom?
opts: Small airways snapping open
Deflated small airways snapping open on inspiration produce crackles, which are NON-musical and discontinuous.
Inflamed pleura rubbing together
Roughened pleural surfaces sliding together produce a grating pleural rub, not a musical sound.
Partial lower airway obstruction
Correct: wheezing comes from partial lower airway obstruction, by secretions and tissue inflammation in asthma or by a foreign body.
Narrowing in the larynx or trachea
Narrowing of the upper airway in the larynx or trachea produces stridor, a high-pitched inspiratory whistle over the neck.

set2.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
set2.q: Which procedure is performed through the intercostal space between the 4th and 5th ribs?
opts: Needle decompression of tension pneumothorax
Needle decompression goes in at the 2nd intercostal space anteriorly, well above the 4th to 5th rib space used for chest tubes.
Thoracentesis
Thoracentesis is a posterior procedure: the needle enters the 7th intercostal space, immediately above the 8th rib.
Checking endotracheal tube depth
Endotracheal tube depth is read against T4, the lower margin for the tube on a chest x-ray, not against a rib space.
Chest tube insertion
Correct: the space between the 4th and 5th ribs is the chest tube site, and the triangle of safety in the midaxillary line puts it at the nipple line.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
set2.q: A long-time smoker has had a productive cough with sputum for years, now followed by progressive dyspnea and recurrent chest infections. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Asthma
Asthma is episodic with symptom-free intervals, not a continuous productive cough for years.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is episodic air hunger and sighing at rest or with distress, not a years-long productive cough.
Chronic bronchitis
Correct: chronic bronchitis is a chronic productive cough followed by progressive dyspnea, with sputum, recurrent respiratory infections and wheezing in a smoker.
Interstitial lung disease
Interstitial lung disease has a DRY cough with fatigue and weakness; years of sputum point to chronic bronchitis.

mis.Interstitial lung disease: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
set2.q: A cough has lasted 5 weeks. How is it classified?
opts: Acute
Acute cough lasts less than 3 weeks; at 5 weeks this cough has moved into the subacute range of 3-8 weeks.
Chronic
Chronic means more than 8 weeks; 5 weeks falls within the subacute range of 3-8 weeks.
Episodic
Episodic describes the timing of dyspnea (as in asthma), not a duration class of cough; 5 weeks is subacute.
Subacute
Correct: acute is under 3 weeks, subacute 3-8 weeks and chronic more than 8 weeks, so 5 weeks is subacute.
